Write a note to a friend about what the sharing economy means for how companies are run. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hey Sam,

I've been thinking about the sharing economy lately, and I believe it changes more about how companies are run than most people realize. We usually talk about Uber and Airbnb as consumer stories. But the real shift is happening inside the organization.

Here's the core idea: when anyone can rent out a spare room, a car, or a few hours of their time, the company no longer needs to own everything it uses. Assets, and increasingly people, become something you access rather than hold. That means managers must rethink what they are actually responsible for. (I found Arun Sundararajan's book The Sharing Economy helpful on this point, if you want a place to start.)

Think of it in terms of a simple trade-off: control versus flexibility. In a traditional company, you hire people, give them a role, and direct their work from the top. In a platform model, you set the rules, build the marketplace, and then step back while others do the work. In other words, the manager becomes less of a boss and more of a host.

This has three practical effects, as I see it.

First, trust replaces supervision. Ratings, reviews, and transparent feedback do much of the work that middle management once did. Nobody has to check up on a driver when the customer's rating already tells the story.

Second, talent is no longer tied to a single employer. Many skilled people prefer to work on several projects at once—they want variety and autonomy, not a corner office. Companies that can't offer a meaningful way to collaborate will lose them to those that can.

Third, decisions move closer to the edge. When thousands of participants are contributing, no central team can anticipate every need. The organizations that do well are the ones that let people experiment, share what they learn, and adjust quickly. That sounds a lot like the open organization ideas we've talked about before.

Of course, there are real concerns. Worker protections, fairness, and accountability don't disappear just because an app is in the middle. Leaders will have to build these in deliberately, not hope they appear on their own.

Still, I'm convinced the direction is clear. Companies will own less, trust more, and lead by setting the conditions for others to contribute rather than by giving orders.

I'd love to hear what you think, especially from your vantage point in your own company. Let's grab coffee soon and compare notes.

Talk soon,
[name]
